name: Invoice Capture and Coding
title: Invoice Capture and Coding
answer: Invoice capture and coding is the process of turning supplier invoices, whether paper, PDF, or e-invoice, into structured payable records and assigning the correct general ledger, cost center, tax, and payment terms. It sits inside accounts payable and touches procurement, receiving, treasury, and master data. The work covers header fields, line items, tax amounts, and the coding decisions that route an invoice to the right account and approver. It also includes exception handling for missing purchase orders, mismatched quantities, or unclear descriptions. The output is a ready-to-post invoice or a routed exception, not a payment decision.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Invoice capture and coding is the process of turning supplier invoices, whether paper, PDF, or e-invoice, into structured payable records and assigning the correct general ledger, cost center, tax, and payment terms. It sits inside accounts payable and touches procurement, receiving, treasury, and master data. The work covers header fields, line items, tax amounts, and the coding decisions that route an invoice to the right account and approver. It also includes exception handling for missing purchase orders, mismatched quantities, or unclear descriptions. The output is a ready-to-post invoice or a routed exception, not a payment decision.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on document ingestion services, optical character recognition, and increasingly on large language models or multimodal models that read layout and text together. They connect to ERP and accounting platforms through APIs, often with a queue for human review. Master data such as vendor records, chart of accounts, tax codes, and purchase order history is essential reference data. Storage and processing may be cloud or on premises, and audit logs are part of the stack. Some deployments use robotic process automation to move data between systems that lack direct integration.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The typical pipeline starts with capture, where the system extracts text and layout from the invoice. Then it classifies the document, matches it to a vendor and purchase order, and predicts coding for each line. Confidence scores decide whether the invoice posts automatically or goes to a clerk for review. Rules and machine learning models often work together, with rules handling tax and tolerance checks and models handling free-text descriptions. Feedback from corrections is used to retrain or tune the models over time.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Controls matter because invoice coding affects financial reporting, tax, and vendor payments. Common controls include rules for retention, access, and segregation of duties, plus an audit trail that shows what the model extracted and what a person changed. Provenance includes the source document, the model or rule version, and the reviewer identity. Compliance pages and regulation trackers can help teams follow changing e-invoicing and tax rules, though the site's 222 compliance and regulation pages are a general resource, not legal advice. Risk areas include duplicate payments, fraud, and biased or drifting models that misclassify spend.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward touchless processing for clean, high-volume invoices and more focused human work on exceptions and supplier disputes. E-invoicing mandates and real-time reporting are pushing capture closer to the transaction. Models are becoming better at reading messy documents and suggesting codes from historical patterns. The open questions are how much autonomy to grant, how to explain coding decisions to auditors, and how to keep master data clean enough for automation to work. Expect more integration between capture, procurement, and payment systems rather than standalone tools.
